pages.body:
The paper's first claim about any feature it studies is [[activation-specificity]]: when this unit is on, the hypothesised context is present. This chart exists because that claim turns out not to be one fact but a fact that changes along the firing range, and a chart is the only form that shows the change.

A single percentage is available, and the paper does quote one. Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens and 81% of the tokens where the [[arabic-script-feature]] is active. Split by how hard the feature fired, that same quantity runs from roughly 25% at the bottom of the range to about 98% above an activation of 5 ([[fig-8]]). Averaging over all firings hides the gradient, and the weak firings that drag the average down are also the ones that move the logits least ([[large-activations-dominate]]).

### Reading one column

The horizontal axis is the [[feature-activation]] on a single token — the autoencoder's ReLU hidden value — running from just above zero out to somewhere between 7 and 12 depending on the feature. Exact zeros are not plotted. They live in a small `0`/`>0` control at the far left, because the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] makes hard zeros the overwhelming majority of tokens and a bar for them would flatten everything else.

The vertical axis is a count of sampled tokens. Its magnitude is itself a quantity worth reading: feature panels peak in the thousands to tens of thousands, while the same plot drawn for a neuron peaks around a million.

Colour is a [[computational-proxy]] — a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] evaluated over prefixes ending at the token ([[prefix-maximization]]) and clipped to ±5, deep blue at −5 through white at 0 to deep red at +5. That score is computed from the token string alone. Nothing about it comes from the model, which is what makes the two axes an argument rather than a restatement.

Each column is therefore a small stacked bar, and the claim lives in the red *fraction*, not the height. The thin conditional strip beneath renormalises every column to full height so those fractions can be compared directly. Above sit random examples per activation band ([[annotated-dataset-example-panel]]).

### How much it establishes

Its negative control is the same chart drawn for the [[most-correlated-neuron]], where the strip stays the same colour mixture at every activation ([[fig-14]]).

The cost is that the proxy is a yardstick, not ground truth. Blue at high activation is read as the proxy's failure ([[proxy-limitations]]); blue at low activation gets [[weak-activation-hypotheses]] rather than a measurement. Summarised as one number the picture is unstable — 0.8 for DNA once binarised ([[proxy-binarization]]), 0.55 for Hebrew, 0.38 for base64, with the low ones attributed to a proxy that is too broad ([[feature-proxy-correlation]]). The chart is strongest where it stays a picture, as in the [[universality]] check across [[transformer-a-and-b|the two transformers]] ([[fig-17]]).

This is the shape the paper reaches for whenever the claim is about *which tokens*, not how much. A correlation can say a [[feature]] and an independent [[computational-proxy]] mostly agree; only the text itself can show that the feature fired on the Arabic and stayed off on the English beside it.

### The two things drawn on a token

The orange background is [[feature-activation]] — the ReLU output of one [[sparse-autoencoder]] hidden unit on that token, darker for stronger.

The underline comes from a second forward pass. Run the context up to the MLP, decode the activations into features, then set this one feature's activation to zero at every position in the context. Concretely, subtract its activation times its [[feature-direction]] from the MLP activation vector, and finish the rest of the model ([[feature-ablation]]).

Now compare each token's predicted log-likelihood before and after. Purple means the number went down, so the feature had been helping that prediction. Orange-red means it went up, so the feature had been hurting it. Thickness carries magnitude and the scale is unlabelled ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]), so read underlines against each other inside one figure, not across figures.

[[fig-11]] puts five snippets in each of two columns, one at the top of the [[arabic-script-feature|Arabic feature]]'s range and one at roughly half it ([[activation-interval]]). Arabic glyphs sit on a lower line with their half-character byte tokens above as escape codes ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

### The audit grid

[[fig-21]] reuses the same annotated snippet with no underlines. Four columns are activation levels, each tied by a dotted line to the histogram welded underneath. Two rows are the proxy's yes/no verdict on the [[dna-feature]] after [[proxy-binarization]]. Six random examples fill each cell — random, not top-activating ([[top-dataset-examples]]).

The off-diagonal cells are the point. Six examples have the proxy firing with the feature off; eighteen have the feature firing with the proxy off. The paper reads all twenty-four and calls two of them genuine errors: one miss ([[activation-sensitivity]]) and one false positive ([[activation-specificity]]). The other twenty-two it charges to the proxy — spaces inside triplets, dashes, the `5'-` prefix that predicts DNA without being DNA ([[proxy-limitations]]).

### What it is worth

The cost is that this is counting by hand. The [[pearson-correlation|Pearson correlation]] of $0.8$ between binarized proxy and feature activations is a population number; the tally of twenty-four is a tally of one display, adjudicated by the authors, on features the paper says it picked for being easy to analyze ([[cherry-picked-case-studies]]). "Two genuine errors" is a judgement about a picture, not an error rate.

What a failure would look like is still legible, and that is the panel's defence. Underlines flat grey everywhere would mean the direction is a fact about the data that the MLP never reads. Purple as heavy under Latin tokens as Arabic would sink the interpretation. And a half-activation column with underlines as strong as the top column would break the roughly linear picture the [[logit-weight]] analysis assumes ([[large-activations-dominate]]).

pages.body:
A conceptual schematic in this paper is a drawing with nothing measured in it: no axis, no units, no population to average over. They appear at four points — the problem setup ([[fig-3]]), the standard the case studies are then held to ([[fig-7]]), the geometry of [[feature-splitting]] ([[fig-45]]), and the discussion's pair of sketches asking whether a [[feature]], the interpretable direction the paper wants to decompose the model into, is a single direction at all ([[fig-61]], [[fig-62]]).

### The vocabulary is small and reused

A dot is one unit, and which unit changes with the figure. In [[fig-3]] it is a neuron. In [[fig-7]] it is a token where the feature fired. In the discussion sketches it is a [[feature-direction]] — the unit vector a feature writes along when it fires.

A ring or a blob is a region of a space. [[fig-7]]'s grey circle is the whole training distribution, and its orange ring is the set of tokens a [[computational-proxy]] flags: a score $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$ computed from the text alone, with nothing from the autoencoder in it. The panel asks one question only — do the dots fall inside the ring.

An arrow is either a mapping or a direction. [[fig-3]]'s three orange dashed arrows run downward, meaning the larger imagined network is expressed inside the smaller real one, which is [[superposition]]. [[fig-45]]'s arrows instead all share a tail, because only their angles carry meaning.

Colour separates the operative element from the backdrop. [[fig-45]]'s faint grey arrows are the conjectured [[true-features]], held in the same positions across all three panels, so you watch the bold learned ones multiply against a fixed background.

Then stop. Counting dots invents precision the drawing lacks: [[fig-3]]'s six-into-three squeeze stands for 4,096 dictionary features over 512 MLP neurons, and [[fig-62]]'s ring carries four points because four space evenly around a circle.

### What a drawing can and cannot settle

Each of these claims is a relation — inside or outside, more or fewer, the same territory or new territory, one description or two. Giving it an axis would imply a measurement that does not exist.

The cost is that a schematic cannot be wrong. Falsification lives in the measured figure each one points at.

[[fig-7]]'s first panel draws its own failure: dots scattered with no common region, which is [[polysemanticity]]. Whether a real feature avoids that is settled elsewhere, by an activation spectrum where the Arabic feature's specificity runs from 25% at its weakest activations to 98% above an activation of 5. [[fig-3]] would fail if each neuron were already one clean feature — a [[privileged-basis]] aligned with the model's own units, which would make [[dictionary-learning]] unnecessary.

Distance from evidence varies across the four. [[fig-45]] arrives after the [[feature-umap|UMAP]] that measured it, summarising a result rather than announcing one. [[fig-62]] sits behind a "perhaps", offered as one possible reason splitting never stopped, and why the [[correct-number-of-features]] may not be a well-posed question.

pages.body:
The paper reaches for this shape in section 5.3 when a claim is about thousands of feature pairs at once and no single number can carry it. The claim is [[universality]] — that [[dictionary-learning]] on two separately trained transformers finds the same [[feature|features]] — in its harder form: when you compare features by two different definitions of "the same feature", do the definitions agree on the same pairs?

That is a question about a joint distribution, which is why a scatter and not a pair of averages. Two bar heights would tell you the level of each measure and nothing about pairing, and pairing is the whole question. A table of a few examples invites the suspicion that they were chosen.

### Building the cloud

One dot is **one matched pair of features**. This is the misreading to guard against: the per-feature scatters earlier in the paper, such as [[fig-51]], look nearly identical but put one datapoint or one vocabulary token per dot.

The construction. Take each of the 4,096 hidden units of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] trained on model A. Find, in run B/1 — a dictionary trained on a second one-layer transformer differing only in random seed ([[transformer-a-and-b]]) — the feature whose activations correlate most highly with it. That correlation is [[activation-similarity]], a [[pearson-correlation]] taken over a fixed sample of 40,960,000 tokens.

Every A/1 feature contributes one dot, so the cloud holds a few thousand.

The horizontal axis is always that same activation correlation. It is also the criterion the partner was chosen by, so each point already sits as far right as its A/1 feature could reach. The bottom marginal therefore reads "how good was the best match available", not "how similar are two features in general", and it should lean right. Its median is $0.72$.

The vertical axis is the only free measurement, and the only thing that changes between the two uses. In [[fig-53]] it is [[logit-weight-similarity]]: the correlation of the pair's [[logit-weight]] vectors, indexed by vocabulary token. In [[fig-54]] it is [[attribution-similarity]], over their [[attribution-vector|attribution vectors]] ([[eq-attribution-vector]]).

Both axes are correlations on the same scale, so the diagonal $y = x$ carries meaning. Read the vertical spread against it, then read the left marginal for where the free measure piles up.

### What a bad result would look like

Fig-54 claims attribution correlation tracks activation correlation. It would fail as a round blob with no tilt, or as a band pinned near $1.0$ at every $x$ — a measure that separates nothing.

Fig-53 inverts this. It is drawn to show a gap, so a tight diagonal would have been the null result. Its ringed outlier, activation correlation $0.98$ with a negative logit weight correlation ([[logit-weight-disagreement]]), is kept in view rather than averaged away, and the paper reads it as [[interference]] from [[superposition]] rather than as a bad match.

Colour encodes nothing in either plot. Density of overplotted grey is the only intensity channel; colour appears as annotation only.

### How much it settles

Less than it looks, in one respect the paper does not raise: the attribution vector has the feature's activation as a factor, so some of fig-54's diagonal is built in by construction rather than found.

Neither scatter can say whether $0.72$ is high. That needs the neuron baseline of $0.46$ from the companion histograms ([[feature-vs-neuron-universality]], [[fig-52]]).

Read the two in order. Fig-54 is the repair of fig-53, and the change in cloud shape between them is the argument.

One point is one feature, meaning one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]], and its position comes from that unit's own weights: one column of the [[dictionary-decoder]], one row and one bias entry of the [[autoencoder-encoder]]. The shape gets used where the paper needs a claim about an entire dictionary before anyone has read a single feature's dataset examples, and where the summary number that was available would have hidden the thing being claimed.

### Building the axes

In the decoder-sparsity version, [[fig-63]] from the [[external-replication]], square every entry of the feature's decoder column and divide by their total. The x-coordinate is the largest single share. The y-coordinate is shares two through ten added together.

Both are fractions of the same total, so $x + y \le 1$. And no one of the next nine shares can exceed the top one, so $y \le 9x$. That second bound is the straight diagonal cutting off the upper left, above which no feature can sit.

Colour is a label the replicator assigned by thresholding those same shares — one-neuron, ten-neuron, dense — and the cutoffs are not printed, so it is his reading drawn onto the plot rather than a third measurement. His reported split, 4% of features dominated by a single neuron, 4% by their top ten, 92% neither, is the table version of this picture. The scatter shows those three labels are threshold cuts through one continuous cloud, not three kinds of thing.

The three-diagnostic version, [[fig-66]], uses three axes because no one of them pulls the groups apart alone ([[density-cluster-separation]]). Horizontal is the dot product of a feature's decoder column with its encoder row, which carries information only because the two are learned separately ([[untied-decoder-weights]]). Height is that feature's entry of the encoder bias $\mathbf{b}_e$ in $\mathbf{f} = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$, always negative, readable as a firing threshold. Depth is [[feature-density]] on a $\log_{10}$ scale from $-10$ to $-3$, logarithmic because densities span that many orders of magnitude.

### What failure would look like

If learned features were mostly neurons wearing new names, the fig-63 cloud would pile against the right edge, $x$ near one and $y$ near zero. It does not, and the dense mass sits below $x = 0.2$. That is the population form of what the case studies find one feature at a time ([[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]]), and what [[superposition]] predicts.

The plot does not display the claim attached to it, that the [[privileged-basis]] survives anyway; that one rests on a [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test|kurtosis statistic]] reported in the text.

For fig-66, failure is a gradient instead of an island — continuous shading with no gap, which is what density alone gives in wide runs with a large [[l1-coefficient]] ([[feature-density-histogram]]). Read the shape of the cloud, never one point.

Both plots are single runs, one of them an outside dictionary on a different model, and fig-66 is a 3-D projection shown at a single angle that rotation might close. A clean gap supplies a boundary to draw around the [[high-density-cluster]]. It does not show that the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] on the other side is a training artifact rather than something the transformer really has.

The paper's per-feature case is a fixed set of five claims — the [[feature-evidence-template|five-claim template]] — and each claim arrives in a different unit: a purity fraction, a next-token [[logit-weight]], a correlation against neurons, a firing rate. There is no shared axis, so there is no single plot. What the paper prints instead is a page of its published [[feature-exploration-interface|browser]], with four kinds of evidence about one [[feature]] side by side, so a reader can check whether they agree.

### Reading one page

[[fig-4]] shows feature #3923. The left column holds three ranked tables. NEURON ALIGNMENT decomposes the [[feature-direction]] into the 512 MLP neurons ([[neuron-basis-coefficients]]): the largest coefficient here is neuron 138 at $+0.40$, carrying 3.6% of the direction's $L^1$ mass. CORRELATED NEURONS ranks neurons by how closely their activations track the feature's ([[most-correlated-neuron]]); the best reaches $+0.09$. CORRELATED B FEATURES runs the same comparison against a dictionary trained on [[transformer-a-and-b|a second transformer differing only in seed]] — [[universality]] measured by [[activation-similarity]] — and the best reaches $+0.75$.

Those two numbers are the load-bearing pair. Flip either and the page collapses. A correlated neuron at $0.9$ would mean [[dictionary-learning]] handed back a neuron under a new name. A best B feature at $0.1$ would mean the feature is an artifact of one seed.

The middle column stacks two histograms: [[feature-activation]] counts over sampled tokens with the exact zeros dropped, the firing rate quoted separately as [[feature-density]] (0.144% here), and below it logit weights over the whole vocabulary with the ten strongest tokens listed each way.

Then the [[top-dataset-examples|top 20 activating examples]], and beside them [[activation-interval|eleven evenly spaced bands]] stepping down from the maximum activation of 11.54. The bands are the half that answers [[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example problem]]: an interpretation that holds at the top usually starts failing three bands down.

Colour carries two channels at once. Orange background is activation on that token. The underline is [[feature-ablation|ablation effect]] ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]) — and here trust the figure's own key, since the body text and the appendix name opposite colours for the same direction.

### What the search strip adds

[[fig-5]] carries no results at all. It reads left to right as one query: a match mode, the field matched against (examples, logits, index, or the [[automated-interpretability|machine-written explanation]]), a sort key over every feature, and Underline Mode, choosing whether the underlines mean this one feature ablated or all learned features substituted for the MLP ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]).

That strip is what makes the browser more than illustration. Run A/1 has 4,096 features and the paper discusses four. Sorting by Random hands the check to a reader who can open a feature the authors never mentioned.

The page shown does not hide its weak spots. Its human label reads `Latin: ?`, and its [[activation-prediction-scoring|automated score]] is $0.305$ — above zero, far from a match.

This is the chart the paper draws to check on one trained autoencoder while it is still iterating on technique. It plots [[feature-density]] — the fraction of tokens on which a learned [[feature]] takes a nonzero value — for every feature in the dictionary at once, and it is here because the paper has no test-loss equivalent for [[dictionary-learning]] ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]).

### Reading one chart

One chart covers one [[dictionary-learning-run]] — a single trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], named in the paper's run notation ([[feature-notation]]). Every hidden unit of that autoencoder contributes one count to one bin. So this is a census of a dictionary, not a picture of any one feature.

The x axis is $\log_{10}$ of density. A tick at $-7$ means one token in ten million, and $-5$ one in a hundred thousand. The log axis is forced: the busiest features fire on well under 1% of tokens and the rarest around $10^{-7}$, so a linear axis would stack five orders of magnitude against the origin.

The y axis is a raw count of features per bin, not normalised by dictionary width. In an overlay, a wider run is taller for free, and height alone is not the evidence.

Units that never fire have density exactly $0$, which has no logarithm. [[dead-neurons]] are therefore absent from the chart rather than sitting at its left edge.

The paper reads two numbers off the shape: how many features a run recovered, and how rare the rarest recovered one is. Neither survives being averaged, because the densities are two populations and a mean lands in the gap between them. So look at the left edge first, then for a valley: the narrow spike near $10^{-7}$ is the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], almost none of whose features the paper finds interpretable, and the broad mass to its right is the [[high-density-cluster]], anecdotally almost all interpretable.

### How strong the evidence is

[[fig-64]] is the clean case, run A/16, two modes with a gap; the paper adds that the right mode may itself be splitting, and says it is still investigating. [[fig-65]] is the same shape for the widest run at $131{,}072$ units, where the modes merge and the diagnostic stops working. The paper reports that overlap comes with large dictionaries and a large [[l1-coefficient]], anecdotally and with no threshold, and falls back on [[density-cluster-separation]] ([[fig-66]]).

[[fig-67]] carries the scaling claim: five panels of $\lambda$, six dictionary widths each ([[expansion-factor]] $1\times$ to $256\times$). Within a panel the left edge marches left as the dictionary widens, which the paper reads as not yet having exhausted the model's [[true-features]]. That reading is a hedge, not a proof — counting alone cannot separate a genuinely new rare feature from [[feature-splitting]] of one already found. The interpretability split between the two modes is anecdotal too, with no score reported per mode. What the chart does support firmly is the sparsity check in [[feature-density-diagnostics]], where a pile of features above $10^{-2}$ says the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] is too weak.

The chart draws one column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] coordinate by coordinate: the [[feature-direction]] that the [[sparse-autoencoder]] writes along whenever one feature fires. It appears in section 3.1.4 to settle a negative question, [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]] — did [[dictionary-learning]] find structure the neuron basis did not already hold, or did it hand back a well-behaved neuron under a new name?

What settles that is a count, not a ranking. A bar chart of the ten biggest contributors names the loudest neurons and throws the count away. A single summary number takes similar values for a spike and for a spread. So the paper uses the bar chart that refuses to select: every coordinate gets a mark, at its true signed height.

### Reading it

One stem is one MLP neuron of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], which has 512. The horizontal axis is the neuron's index and nothing else, so its ordering carries no information.

The vertical axis is that neuron's entry in the feature's decoder column. These are [[neuron-basis-coefficients]]. Read a stem as how much of that neuron's activation the feature adds when it is on — not as how strongly the neuron responds to the feature's context. MLP activations are non-negative, so a negative stem means the feature pushes that neuron down.

The scale misleads. Columns are held at [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]], so the 512 squared coefficients sum to $1$. That fixes two reference marks. A feature that *is* a neuron shows one stem at $\pm 1$ and 511 flat. A feature spread evenly shows every stem at $1/\sqrt{512} \approx 0.044$. So $0.044$ is the yardstick for "large", not $1.0$, and the paper's cutoff of $0.1$ is a little over twice it — chosen, not derived.

### What it shows, and how far it carries

For the [[arabic-script-feature|Arabic script feature]], [[fig-13]] gives 27 coefficients past $0.1$, and the three largest by magnitude are negative. Sign is doing work here. A negative coefficient is invisible to a scan of neurons' top activating examples, which is the section's other check ([[top-dataset-example-search]]).

The falsifying picture is easy to draw: one stem near $0.9$ and the rest flat would say the autoencoder relabelled a neuron, and that for this feature the [[polysemanticity]] problem was never there.

The evidence is thinner than the conclusion, and the paper says so. Spread coefficients could still cancel so as to sharpen one neuron, and this plot cannot rule that out. That is why the argument moves on to the [[most-correlated-neuron]] over roughly 40 million examples. It is also one chart, for one hand-picked feature — an existence proof that some features are [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis|invisible in the neuron basis]], not a claim about the population.

The population version comes later, in the [[external-replication]]: 92% of features spread rather than concentrated, alongside a [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]] arguing that the neuron basis is still a [[privileged-basis]] anyway. Both are pictures of what [[superposition]] predicts.

Every other chart in the paper scores one unit at a time. This shape draws several [[feature|features]] as boxes with labelled edges between them, because two of the paper's claims are about pairs of features and dissolve when written out one feature at a time.

There are no axes; position is layout. One exception: in the splitting graph the horizontal is an ordered sweep of [[dictionary-learning-run]]s — $512$, $4{,}096$, $16{,}384$ features, the same transformer underneath, only the width of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] changing.

A box is one feature, named by [[feature-notation]] as model / run / index, the index arbitrary. What fills it is evidence, not decoration. In the automaton figures it is a strip of [[top-dataset-examples]], orange marking the [[feature-activation]] on each token, darker for stronger ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). In the splitting graph it is a single line of human description.

### The two kinds of edge

In the automaton figures an arrow is not a weight and not a wire. Its label lists the source feature's largest positive [[logit-weight]] entries — the tokens its firing pushes hardest in the next-token distribution. It points at the feature those tokens switch on one position later.

The handoff travels through emitted text. Nothing inside the model joins the two features ([[finite-state-automata-features]]).

So read an arrow's token list, then read the orange tokens in the box it lands on. The same tokens? Then the arrow is earned. Then check whether you return where you started. A dashed arrow leaving the diagram marks a predicted token that no node on the page accounts for.

In the splitting graph an edge means only that a [[masked-cosine-similarity]] cleared a threshold. Take the cosine between two features' activations over the tokens where the first fires, take it again over the tokens where the second fires, keep the larger, and draw a line above roughly $0.4$. The paper says that threshold was chosen for display. Colour marks which coarse feature a branch descends from, nothing else.

### What a weak version looks like

For the automata: arrows whose labelled tokens are not the tokens the target box highlights, or no closed cycle, or labels made of high-frequency tokens that any feature would promote.

Nothing here is an intervention. Both ends of every arrow are truncated top-$k$ lists read off the feature interface — no ablation, no measurement that emitting the token raises the target's activation. The tidiness is resolution-dependent too: A/0 holds 512 features for a 512-dimensional space, so it is not overcomplete ([[overcompleteness]]), and the paper says wider runs split each node into a family.

For the splitting graph: children no narrower than their parents, or a threshold no sweep is shown for.

[[fig-58]] is the reference case, four A/0 features cycling through HTML ([[html-feature-automaton]]). [[fig-57]] runs the shape twice on Unicode, where a character arrives as a prefix byte plus a suffix byte ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]], [[unicode-token-state-machines]]). [[fig-46]] keeps the boxes and changes what an edge means, tracing [[feature-splitting]] across widths and finding one node with two parents ([[splitting-is-not-a-tree]]).

pages.body:
Every population-scale claim in this paper that learned directions beat neurons is made with this one chart shape. Two histograms are drawn on a shared horizontal axis: one for the roughly 3,676 [[feature|features]] of a [[sparse-autoencoder|sparse autoencoder]] run, one for the 512 MLP neurons of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer transformer]] those features were fit to, with each unit collapsed to a single number.

It exists because the paper's four detailed case studies are, by its own admission, [[cherry-picked-case-studies|chosen for being easy to analyse]]. A histogram puts every scored unit in the picture instead.

### Reading one

The horizontal axis is whichever score that figure uses, computed once per unit. A "unit" is either one dictionary direction or one MLP neuron, written in [[neuron-notation|the A/neurons/N form]] so the two never get confused.

The vertical axis is usually density, not count. Each population is normalised separately to enclose area 1, because 3,676 against 512 would otherwise flatten the neurons into nothing. So bar height carries no information about how many units were scored.

To recover a share of a population, multiply height by bin width. A bar of height $4$ over bins of width $0.02$ covers $4 \times 0.02 = 0.08$, about eight percent of that population.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, yellow marks the [[randomized-transformer|randomised-weight baseline]] where it appears. Dark navy is not a third group — it is the two translucent fills overlapping, and navy area is evidence against the claim.

Read the small triangles under the axis first. Those are medians, and the gap between them is the whole argument.

### Why a distribution, and what it hides

A mean would have buried the result the paper most wants shown. On the hand-scored figure neurons average about 3.2 while their median is 0 — most neurons scored nothing at all, and a thin tail pulled the average up. A distribution shows whether a gap is a whole population shifted or a minority doing the work.

### How strong this actually is

[[manual-interpretability-scoring|The hand-scored arm]] ([[fig-39]]) is the paper's most trusted evidence and its smallest: 412 [[activation-interval|activation intervals]] across 162 units, scored by a single [[blinded-annotation|blinded]] rater who is one of the authors, on a [[feature-interpretability-rubric|0–14 rubric]]. Medians 12 against 0.

[[automated-interpretability|The automated arms]] scale but weaken. [[fig-40]] scores explanation-driven activation prediction by [[spearman-correlation|Spearman correlation]]; [[fig-41]] scores [[automated-logit-scoring|logit-token prediction]] at 74% for features against 58% for neurons, over a 50% chance line — a real gap, but neurons are already well above chance.

[[fig-52]] reuses the shape for [[universality]], with [[pearson-correlation|activation correlation]] to the nearest match in a separately seeded model: 0.72 against 0.46.

[[fig-71]] is the honest one. Reweighting by [[importance-scoring]] slumps both populations toward zero, and the paper prints it rather than dropping it.

pages.body:
Every other interpretability number here is one score per unit, summed over a whole [[feature-interpretability-rubric|rubric]]. This chart takes a single line item of that rubric and spreads it along a second axis — how hard the unit was firing — to ask whether the interpretation an annotator settled on holds across a unit's whole range, or only at its top.

The worry it answers is specific. The standard way to read a unit is to pull its [[top-dataset-examples|top-activating dataset examples]] and read off what they share. The paper thinks that method flatters [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] units, which often look clean at their maximum and mixed further down ([[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example weakness]]).

### Making the bands

Take one unit and find its maximum activation. Cut the range from zero to that maximum into eleven evenly spaced [[activation-interval|activation intervals]], and draw examples uniformly from each band rather than from the top.

Each unit is cut against its own peak. A [[feature]] whose maximum is 9 and one whose maximum is 0.6 both feed the `~50%` column, and the axis never means an absolute activation.

The scoring runs in a fixed order. The annotator first commits to one interpretation of the unit, formed from all intervals plus its positive logit weights. Then rubric item three — zero to five, how consistent a band's strongly-firing tokens are with that interpretation — is scored band by band.

A low band score therefore does not say the band is confusing on its own. It says the band disagrees with the story already committed to. Features from the [[sparse-autoencoder|autoencoder]] and the transformer's own [[neuron-notation|MLP neurons]] both go through this, [[blinded-annotation|with the annotator not told which is which]].

### What it carries

[[fig-42]] plots the per-band means. Both curves climb with activation strength. Neurons climb too, so the rise is a property of firing hard, not something [[dictionary-learning]] bought.

The cost is sample size. Hand scoring produced 412 intervals in all, so a band holds roughly 37 across both populations — a mean drawn from a couple of dozen integer scores.

Read the crossing loosely. Features start near 2.6 in the lowest band and pass the dotted line at 3 around `~20%`, but the label calls that line subjective; move it to 4 and the crossing slides to `~40%`. The gap between the two curves is the sturdier evidence.

The paper's prose is more careful than the average line. Many features stay consistent across the whole spectrum; others hold across the top ~60% and then fall away fast. One curve mixes those two populations, and the paper explains the weak end only by guessing that a direction learned [[feature-at-slight-angle|at a slight angle]] to the true one would misbehave there.

That weak end is where the result is thinnest. [[low-interval-activation-skew|Most real activations are small]], so most land in the worst-scoring bands. The paper's answer — [[large-activations-dominate|large activations carry most of the effect]] on the output — argues about where a feature's influence lives, not that its quiet firings are interpretable.

pages.body:
This is the first of the paper's three checks on what a feature does rather than when it fires ([[feature-downstream-effects]]). It is here because [[dictionary-learning]] is fit to the MLP activations and nothing else, so a sceptic can say the [[feature|features]] are structure in the training data rather than anything the model computes ([[model-vs-data-question]]).

Logit weights are the reply. They never enter the autoencoder's objective ([[downstream-effects-outside-dictionary-learning]]), so an interpretable one is not something the training could have arranged.

One observation here is one vocabulary entry, not one token of sampled text, and no text is run at all. The chart reuses the legend and colour strip of the [[activation-spectrum-by-proxy|activation histogram]], which makes the two easy to confuse.

### The number being counted

Take the [[feature-direction]] $\mathbf{d}_i$, the unit vector the feature writes along. Push it through the [[mlp-output-weights]] into the residual stream. Apply a [[layer-norm-linearization|linearised layer norm]], then the [[unembedding-matrix]].

That product, $d_i W_{down} \pi L W_{unembed}$, is a [[path-expansion-logit-attribution|single traced path]] from the feature to the output. It gives one [[logit-weight]] per token: how much one unit of the feature's activation adds to that token's next-token logit.

The x axis runs roughly $-0.6$ to $0.6$. It has no absolute zero, since softmax is shift-invariant, so the paper slides each feature's weights until the median is $0$ ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]). Extremely rare and never-used entries are dropped ([[anomalous-token-exclusion]]).

Tens of thousands of numbers rule out a bar chart, and the centering makes a mean uninformative. A table of top-weighted tokens fails differently. The claim is not "the top tokens are Arabic" but that the vocabulary splits in two, and a table cannot say whether its last row sits above the bulk or inside it. So the y axis is density, in vocabulary entries per unit of weight, peaking around 0.2–0.4M.

Colour comes from outside the histogram. Each token string is scored by a [[computational-proxy]] of [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy|log-likelihood-ratio form]], clipped to $\pm 5$, and each column is stacked by that score.

### Where the claim lives

Not in the tall mode at zero. That is nearly the whole vocabulary, and the paper's label on it is "Interference Weights?", question mark included — a guess that it is cross-talk forced by [[superposition]] ([[weight-interference]]). The result is the small [[logit-weight-second-mode]] out near $0.3$–$0.5$, small enough to need an inset ([[fig-10]]).

A failure looks like [[fig-15]]: one mode, with the Arabic tokens of the [[most-correlated-neuron]] spread from about $-0.25$ to $+0.32$, "very slightly positive leaning overall, but some are negative". Or [[fig-31]], where a second mode exists but holds 'htm', 'png', 'pdf'. Both read as [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]], consistent with [[polysemanticity]].

Two things the shape cannot settle, and the paper says so ([[logit-weight-caveats]]). The weights may be too small to matter once multiplied by real activations. The feature may only fire where other features already rule those tokens out. [[feature-ablation]] and [[pinned-feature-sampling]] are there to cover that gap.

The same shape recurs for DNA ([[fig-22]]), base64 ([[fig-26]]) and Hebrew ([[fig-34]]), and again for the matched features in a second transformer, which were selected on activation correlation alone ([[universality]], [[fig-18]]).

Every interpretability score in this paper is one the paper invented, and there is no ground truth to check any of them against. This grid is the reply to the objection that follows: instead of defending one score, it crosses several scores against several populations of units and asks whether the same ranking falls out of all of them.

The ranking being defended is not a number. It is that [[dictionary-learning]] [[feature|features]] are easier to interpret than the transformer's own MLP neurons, which the paper expects to be [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]].

### Reading the grid

In [[fig-69]] the rows are scoring methods and the columns are populations. The three columns are the same all the way down: the 4,096 features of run A/1 ([[feature-notation]]), the 512 MLP neurons of that same transformer, and features learned from a [[randomized-transformer]] whose weight matrices had their entries shuffled in place ([[weight-shuffling]]).

Row 1 is the [[manual-interpretability-scoring|blinded human scoring]], on the $0$–$14$ [[feature-interpretability-rubric]]. It is drawn as raw counts, because the sample is small — 412 [[activation-interval|activation intervals]] across 162 units. Medians: $12$ for features, $0$ for neurons, $7$ for randomized features.

Rows 2 and 3 are the *same* [[automated-interpretability]] experiment scored twice, once with [[pearson-correlation]] and once with [[spearman-correlation]]. Pearson gives $0.52 / 0.25 / 0.62$; Spearman gives $0.57 / 0.18 / 0.61$. The two rows should be read against each other directly, and the paper's point is that the shapes barely move.

Row 4 is [[automated-logit-scoring]], an accuracy where $0.5$ is chance: $0.74 / 0.53 / 0.50$. Rows 2–4 plot density rather than count, so panels holding very different numbers of units are still comparable, and the dotted line marks that row's null value.

The shapes carry as much as the medians. Several panels have a spike sitting exactly on zero, because a constant prediction has no defined correlation and is assigned zero ([[constant-prediction-zero-score]]). A mean over that would say nothing, which is why medians are marked with triangles and the whole histogram is left visible behind them.

### The cell that goes the wrong way

On the activation score the randomized features take the higher median. The paper leaves this in and labels it. [[fig-70]] recolours the same comparison by population and splits the awkward panel on whether a unit is a [[single-token-features|single-token feature]], which reverses the order on the remainder ([[randomized-feature-bimodality]]).

That split was chosen after the result was seen, which is worth holding onto. So is the fact that rows 2 and 3 are one experiment, not two: the crossing is narrower than a four-by-three grid looks, and the human row — the paper's most trusted grader — is the smallest sample in it.

pages.body:
This is [[fig-68]], the one chart in the paper where a hyperparameter choice is shown as a price rather than a ranking. It is here because the paper reports having no single number that says whether [[dictionary-learning]] is working, so it triangulates from several imperfect proxies ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]) — and two of those proxies pull against each other.

### The two numbers carried on each dot

The horizontal axis is the average [[l0-norm]]: the mean count of features with a nonzero activation on a token, running from about 4 to 20. Left is sparser. This rewards a code where almost nothing fires.

The vertical axis is the share of the MLP layer's loss contribution the reconstruction recovers ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]). Walk the computation. Run the transformer, pass its MLP activations through the autoencoder, and splice the reconstruction back in place of the real activations. Measure how much the loss rises. Divide that rise by the rise you get from zeroing the MLP outright ([[zero-ablation-baseline]]), then subtract from one. The axis is labelled "Percent" but ticked in fractions, so 0.95 means 95%.

That second number rewards a code that reproduces the layer. Either axis alone is gameable: rank runs by explained loss and the densest dictionary wins, rank by sparsity and the emptiest does.

One dot is not a feature. It is a whole trained [[sparse-autoencoder]] — one [[dictionary-learning-run]], width and penalty fixed, against the same one-layer transformer.

### Two knobs pointing in different directions

Colour encodes the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$ on the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]]: 0.004, 0.006, 0.008, 0.01. Each line joins six dictionary sizes, 512 up to 131,072 ([[expansion-factor]]); it is a connector, not a fit.

Read the horizontal gaps between colours first. The penalty fixes which vertical band a run lands in — $\lambda = 0.01$ near 4 to 7 active features, $\lambda = 0.004$ near 16 to 20 — and the bands barely overlap.

Then read upward inside one band. A 256-fold wider dictionary climbs the 0.01 band from about 0.67 to 0.89 while $L^0$ shifts by under three.

So the two knobs are not the same lever, and the plot exists to show that. The cost side is just as visible: 0.004's best point, 0.945, buys about 1.5 points over 0.006's 0.93 for roughly double the active features.

### How much this actually settles

Not much, and the appendix does not pretend otherwise. No optimum is derived — only a stated habit of targeting $L^0$ below 10 or 20, and distrusting codes whose $L^0$ is a large fraction of the layer's 512 dimensions ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]]).

The y-values are called overestimates, since zero-ablating the MLP may be an unusually bad baseline ([[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat]]). The $\lambda = 0.001$ runs are dropped to keep the scale readable, which crops out the dense end entirely. And the same sweep grid, shown as [[feature-density-histogram|density histograms]] and again through [[feature-splitting]], suggests widening mostly turns up rarer and finer features — so climbing a band is not closing in on a complete account.

The chart is a scatter in which every dot is one learned feature's dictionary vector, and the only thing it encodes is which features point in similar directions. It is here because the paper's feature families — several base64 features, several Arabic script features, over a hundred features for the token "the" — were assembled by a person reading activating examples, and the paper wants to know whether the [[sparse-autoencoder]] put them near each other in activation space too, without ever being asked to.

### What is actually plotted

One dot is one [[feature-direction]]: a single column of the decoder matrix $W_d$ ([[dictionary-decoder]]), the direction that feature writes into the 512-dimensional MLP activation space of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] when it fires. Not an activation, not a firing rate, not a strength.

Those columns are held at L2 norm 1 ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]). So two features differ only in the angle between their vectors, and cosine is the distance the projection is given to preserve.

[[umap]] takes each of those 512-number vectors down to two, with `metric="cosine"`, `n_neighbors=15`, and `min_dist=0.05` in [[fig-1]] or `0.01` in [[fig-44]].

Count what goes in. Fig-1 embeds two runs jointly, A/0 and A/1, which is $512 + 4{,}096 = 4{,}608$ points. Fig-44 adds A/2's 16,384 features to the same fit, for 20,992 points — same transformer, same sparsity coefficient, only the [[expansion-factor]] changing across 1x, 8x and 32x.

Both axes are UMAP output coordinates: no units, no orientation, no meaning if you refit. Read co-location and nothing else. The width of a gap between two blobs is not a distance.

Fig-1 is one colour, with clusters supplied separately by [[hdbscan-feature-clustering]] and its list ordered by [[one-dimensional-umap-ordering]]. Fig-44 drops the labels and colours instead by [[dictionary-learning-run]], which is the change that makes [[feature-splitting]] legible: at a labelled knot like [[arabic-script-feature|the Arabic script features]] or [[base64-feature|the base64 ones]], one oversized grey A/0 marker sits as a halo under a spray of finer green points.

### How much it shows

A dictionary with no such structure would project to one diffuse ball, because random unit vectors in 512 dimensions are close to mutually orthogonal. The island far to the right — [[ultralow-density-cluster]] features and [[dead-neurons]] — is roughly that picture already, so the null result is visible in the same frame.

The cost is that UMAP will draw clusters out of almost any input, and the paper shows no shuffled or randomised control. The map corroborates the families found by reading text; on its own it does not establish them. The paper's own wording stays at that level — the qualitative clusters are reflected in the geometry of the dictionary ([[feature-geometry-clusters]]).

The penalty is the second of the two terms in the autoencoder's [[sparse-autoencoder-loss|training objective]]: add up the feature activations produced on a datapoint, multiply the total by a scalar, and charge it to the loss. It is there because the [[mse-reconstruction-term|reconstruction term]] on its own would not select anything worth reading.

The dictionary is [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]] — the hidden layer has more units than the vector it is rebuilding. The thing being rebuilt is one 512-dimensional post-ReLU MLP activation at a single token position, and the hidden layer runs from 512 units up to 131,072, with most analyses using the 8× run at 4,096 ([[fig-2]], [[table-1]]). A layer that wide can reconstruct its 512 inputs exactly using dense codes with every unit slightly on, and such a code says nothing about the model. The penalty is what rules that solution out, and it does so by assuming what [[superposition]] predicts: that only a few of the model's features are live at once ([[feature-sparsity]]).

### What the term does to a gradient step

$$\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|X|}\sum_\mathbf{x} \|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{f}\|_1$$

The encoder's ReLU makes every entry of $\mathbf{f}$ non-negative, so $\|\mathbf{f}\|_1$ is simply their sum ([[eq-autoencoder-loss]]). Its gradient with respect to an active feature is the constant $\lambda$, whatever that feature's current value. So a feature earning less reconstruction improvement than $\lambda$ gets pushed down until the ReLU clips it, at which point it is exactly zero rather than merely small.

One asymmetry is worth holding onto: the squared error is a mean over the 512 vector elements, while the L1 is a sum over all 4,096 hidden units. What $\lambda$ means numerically therefore depends on both widths — the paper's 131,072-wide run A/5 uses $\lambda = 0.004$, and [[l1-coefficient|the coefficient]] is one of the two things it varies across runs.

There is an obvious way to cheat this. Since only activations are charged, the decoder could scale its columns up and its activations down, paying less penalty for the same reconstruction. [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns|Fixing every dictionary column to unit norm]] closes that route.

### What the sparsity costs

Because the objective is squared error and not cross-entropy, the paper argues the pressure genuinely discourages the dictionary from packing features into [[superposition-all-the-way-down|superposition of its own]].

The price is reconstruction. Raising $\lambda$ lowers the [[l0-norm|number of features active per token]] and raises the loss when the reconstruction is spliced back into the transformer, and the paper reads [[l0-nll-tradeoff|that frontier]] to choose a setting rather than deriving one. Its main run recovers [[loss-recovered-by-features|79% of the MLP's loss contribution]]; a lower coefficient with far more features reaches 94.5%.

A subtler cost: a [[local-code|local code]], with one unit per combination, is sparser than a [[compositional-code|compositional]] one, so the penalty rewards exactly the representation that would be an artifact. That is the paper's own first hypothesis for its hundreds of [[token-in-context-features|token-in-context features]].

The direct evidence here is thin, and mostly argued rather than measured. No run is shown with the penalty removed. What the figures show is that features trained under it come out specific — the [[dna-feature]] correlates 0.8 with a hand-built proxy ([[fig-20]]), the [[base64-feature]] likewise ([[fig-25]]) — which is downstream of the penalty working, not a test of it. The paper also names sparsity-promoting alternatives to L1 as [[algorithmic-improvements-for-sparse-autoencoders|open work]].

The paper wants to cut a language model into parts small enough to read one at a time. Its opening argument is that the parts the architecture already hands you — the neurons — are the wrong ones, and that there is a reason for this rather than an accident.

### The unit that doesn't work

[[mechanistic-interpretability|Mechanistic interpretability]] is the program of breaking a network into components simpler than the whole, then reasoning about how those components interact. The pressure to decompose at all is [[curse-of-dimensionality-in-interpretability|the curse of dimensionality]]. The volume of internal-state space grows exponentially with model size, and the authors say they see no way to search such a space unless it splits into pieces each of which can be understood on its own.

Neurons are the obvious pieces. But a neuron will often fire on a grab-bag of unrelated inputs — [[classic-polysemantic-neuron-examples|citations, dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean]] in the same unit. The paper calls this [[polysemanticity]]. A unit like that has no single description, so no description of it composes into a description of the network. What the paper wants instead is [[monosemanticity]]: a unit where one interpretation covers both when it fires and what it does.

### Why the neurons are like that

The explanation the paper carries in from its own earlier [[toy-models-of-superposition|Toy Models of Superposition]] is [[superposition]]. A network represents more independent features than it has neurons by giving each feature its own linear combination of neurons rather than its own neuron.

The mechanism offered for this is [[noisy-simulation]]: the small network we can inspect behaves like a squeezed-down projection of a much larger, much sparser network, whose units would each be one clean thing [[fig-3]].

That squeeze is affordable only because of [[feature-sparsity]]. Only a handful of features are active on any given token. So directions that are not orthogonal rarely fire at the same moment, and the cost stays occasional. If many features fired at once, the cross-talk would be constant instead.

Packing more directions than dimensions is [[overcompleteness]], and cross-talk is what the paper calls [[interference]]. Seen from one neuron, this is the whole story: the neuron sits on several feature directions at once, so it lights up on several unrelated things. Polysemanticity is what superposition looks like locally.

### The unit the paper wants instead

The replacement unit is a [[feature]]: a basic interpretable direction in activation space. That directions are the right currency is the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]], which the paper supports by citation and precedent rather than by proving here.

The formal version is [[linear-feature-decomposition|a linear decomposition]] — each activation vector written as a bias plus a sum of unit [[feature-direction|directions]] scaled by their [[feature-activation|activations]] [[eq-feature-decomposition]]. Note what this settles in advance. A feature is a direction by construction, because the factorization has nowhere to put a property the model represents some other way.

Neurons are not arbitrary either. The elementwise nonlinearity singles them out as a [[privileged-basis]], so features have some pull toward the neuron axes — enough that a few neurons read cleanly, not enough that most do [[fig-13]].

Could you just train the superposition away? That was one of [[three-approaches-to-superposition|three strategies]] Toy Models laid out, and the paper reports abandoning it. Forcing [[activation-sparsity-training|activation sparsity during training]] does remove superposition, and the neurons stay polysemantic anyway, because [[cross-entropy-favors-polysemanticity|cross-entropy rewards an ambiguous neuron over a clean one]].

So the decomposition has to be found after training. The paper then fixes what would count as a good one: [[good-decomposition-desiderata|three criteria]] — [[interpretable-activation-conditions|you can say what makes each feature fire]], [[interpretable-downstream-effects|you can say what changing it does downstream]], and [[explaining-the-mlp-layer|the features account for a real share of the layer's loss]].

Those three are the scorecard for everything that follows. The next question is how to actually fit such a decomposition, which the paper answers with [[dictionary-learning]] and a [[sparse-autoencoder]] [[fig-2]].

What exactly is being taken apart, and what is doing the taking apart? Two models are in play, and nearly every later claim depends on keeping them straight.

### The model being read

The subject is [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|a one-layer transformer]] with a 128-dimensional [[residual-stream|residual stream]], one attention block, and an MLP block of 512 ReLU neurons.

One layer is not just a convenient size. Earlier work could analyse a one-layer *attention-only* transformer by rewriting it so that no hidden state ever had to be named. Adding a ReLU MLP breaks that rewrite. So the MLP activation vector is [[mlp-activations-as-target|the state you cannot get around decomposing]], and [[fig-2]] pins down which tensor that is: the 512 post-ReLU numbers at a single token position.

Two training choices are singled out. The model is trained on [[pile-dataset|the Pile]], so the run can be reproduced. And it runs for 100 billion tokens, far past compute-optimal — [[overtraining]] offered as a hypothesis that long training gives cleaner representations, not as a measured effect. [[table-1]] sets both specifications side by side. A second transformer, [[transformer-a-and-b|model B]], differs only in seed, and is held back for the universality checks.

### Why the decomposition must be overcomplete

The reason not to just read the 512 neurons is [[superposition]]: the layer is thought to carry more features than it has neurons, each feature getting a direction rather than a neuron ([[fig-3]]).

So the decomposition writes each activation as a bias plus a weighted sum of unit [[feature-direction|feature directions]] ([[eq-feature-decomposition]]), with more directions than the space has dimensions. That last part, [[overcompleteness]], is what makes this [[dictionary-learning]] rather than the usual search for disentangled dimensions. It has a price: the extra directions cannot all be orthogonal, so features bleed into each other as [[interference]].

The inner problem is recovering a sparse high-dimensional vector from a low-dimensional projection. That is [[compressed-sensing]], and solving it exactly is [[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery|NP-hard]]. Asking for sparsity at all rests on [[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables|the old hypothesis]] that the latent variables behind natural data are mostly off at any moment.

The paper tried [[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms|the established iterative methods]] and set them aside. Partly for scale. Partly out of a worry that a method that strong could pull out structure the transformer itself has no way to read, whereas a [[sparse-autoencoder]] is about as capable as the MLP layer it reads.

### The tool, and the details that matter

The [[autoencoder-encoder|encoder]] is a linear map, a bias, and a ReLU, producing one non-negative number per dictionary element ([[eq-encoder]]). The [[dictionary-decoder|decoder]] maps those numbers back, and its columns are the feature directions — hence "decoder" and "dictionary" used interchangeably.

Training minimizes [[sparse-autoencoder-loss|two terms]] ([[eq-autoencoder-loss]]). The [[mse-reconstruction-term|squared reconstruction error]] wants the dictionary to keep the information. The [[l1-sparsity-penalty|L1 penalty]] on the feature activations wants almost all of them at exactly zero. They pull opposite ways, and [[l1-coefficient|the coefficient $\lambda$]] sets the exchange rate.

That penalty only means something given one constraint. If a dictionary column could grow, the autoencoder could halve every activation and double the column, leaving the reconstruction untouched while the L1 term fell. So the columns are held at [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns|unit norm]].

Note what is *not* in the loss: [[activations-only-decomposition|nothing about the model's outputs]]. That omission is deliberate. It is what lets the later logit and ablation checks count as evidence rather than as circularity.

Two training details are flagged as load-bearing. The [[pre-encoder-bias|pre-encoder bias]], tied to the negative of the decoder bias, is listed as the most important departure from a textbook autoencoder. And [[neuron-resampling]] revives [[dead-neurons|units that have stopped firing]], aiming them at the datapoints currently reconstructed worst, so the dictionary does not waste capacity.

Finally, [[feature-notation|the naming scheme]]: A/1/3450 is model A, dictionary run 1, feature 3450, while A/neurons/489 is a raw MLP neuron.

You can now read any identifier in the paper, and ask what the next section takes up: what does one of these features turn out to be?

pages.body:
A dictionary can be sparse, reconstruct the activations well, and still hand back 4,096 directions nobody can describe. This theme is the paper's answer to a reader who points at one direction and asks how you would ever know what it is.

The answer is a fixed checklist, applied four times. [[feature-evidence-template|Five claims]] are attempted for each feature: it fires only in its hypothesized context, it fires whenever that context is present, it changes the model's output in a way that matches, it is not a neuron under a new name, and a separately trained model grows one like it. [[arabic-script-feature|A/1/3450]], which fires on Arabic script, is walked through all five in order, and the three later case studies reuse that order.

### Specificity needs a yardstick from outside

Claim one carries the most weight. [[activation-specificity|Specificity]] says that when the feature is on, the context is there — and that is what rules out [[polysemanticity]], because a polysemantic unit fires on things with nothing in common.

You cannot check that using the feature itself. So the paper hand-builds a [[computational-proxy]]: a cheap score for whether a string looks like Arabic script, or DNA, or base64. Every proxy has [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy|the same form]] — how much likelier the string is under the hypothesis than under the corpus as a whole ([[eq-proxy-loglikelihood-ratio]]). It reads Unicode blocks and character counts. It never sees the autoencoder, and that is the whole point of it.

Now the comparison means something. Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens, and 81% of the tokens where A/1/3450 is active ([[fig-7]]).

That one number hides a slope. Colouring the activation histogram by the proxy ([[fig-8]]) puts barely-active tokens at roughly 25% Arabic and tokens above activation 5 at about 98%. The paper argues the clean top end is the half that counts, because [[large-activations-dominate|large activations move the logits most]] — in a one-layer model a feature's push on the output is close to [[linear-logit-effects|linear in its activation]]. Reweighting each bar by activation magnitude gives the [[expected-value-plot|expected value plot]] ([[fig-9]]), where almost all the mass is Arabic.

[[activation-sensitivity|Sensitivity]] is the softer half, and the paper says so plainly. A/1/3450 skips the definite-article prefix "ال" every time; [[complementary-arabic-features|other Arabic features]] fire in exactly those gaps. The [[feature-proxy-correlation|feature–proxy correlation]], 0.74 here, folds both halves into one number.

### From firing to doing

Claim three asks whether the model uses the feature. It is checked three ways ([[feature-downstream-effects]]): the [[logit-weight]] histogram grows a small far-right mode of Arabic tokens ([[fig-10]]); [[feature-ablation|ablating]] the feature hurts Arabic predictions across its whole range ([[fig-11]]); and [[pinned-feature-sampling|pinning]] it at maximum turns a counting prefix into Arabic script ([[fig-12]]). None of this was an input to [[dictionary-learning]], which only ever saw MLP activations.

Claim four checks that the dictionary did not just relabel a good neuron ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]). The direction spreads over 27 of 512 coefficients, the three largest negative ([[fig-13]]), and the [[most-correlated-neuron|most correlated neuron]] fires on a grab-bag of non-English languages ([[fig-14]]). Claim five finds B/1/1334 in a separately seeded model at activation correlation 0.91 ([[fig-17]]).

The other three cases vary one thing each. [[dna-feature|DNA]] is a context served by one feature rather than a family ([[fig-20]]). [[base64-feature|Base64]] tests a hunch about universality, and exposes a proxy so broad it counts hexadecimal too ([[fig-25]]). [[hebrew-feature|Hebrew]] shows the proxy failing on shared punctuation rather than the feature failing ([[fig-33]]).

You can now read any of these five claims as an argument rather than a chart. What you cannot do is generalise: the paper states outright that these four were [[cherry-picked-case-studies|chosen for being easy to proxy]], which is why the next move is [[global-analysis-framing|to the whole population]].

The last section's four features were chosen because they were easy to analyse, and the paper says so [[cherry-picked-case-studies]]. So [[global-analysis-framing|the question now]] is whether the typical feature looks anything like them, and whether it beats the neuron it is meant to replace.

### Scoring a population, not a favourite

First, how units get judged has to be fixed. The usual method collects the datapoints where a unit fires hardest and reads off what they share [[top-dataset-examples]]. A [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] neuron often looks coherent at its maximum and turns into a mixture further down, so top examples alone would grade it monosemantic — the weakness the paper [[max-dataset-example-bias|sets out to correct]].

The fix is to sample the whole range. Each unit's activations are cut into eleven evenly spaced bands from zero to its maximum, and examples are drawn from each: an [[activation-interval]].

Those bands are the unit of the human experiment. In [[manual-interpretability-scoring|the manual analysis]], one annotator — an author — scored 412 intervals across 162 features and neurons, without being shown which kind of unit was on screen [[blinded-annotation]]. The [[feature-interpretability-rubric]] runs 0 to 14, summing confidence in an interpretation with how consistent the strong activations and the positive [[logit-weight|logit weights]] are with it, and how specific it is. The median neuron scores 0 — no hypothesis at all. The median feature interval scores 12 [[fig-39]]. It is the number the paper trusts most, and it rests on one rater and a small sample.

Scoring bands separately buys a second result [[activation-interval-analysis]]. Interpretability drops as activations weaken: features clear the annotator's threshold only from roughly the 20% band upward [[fig-42]]. One suggested reason: a direction sitting [[feature-at-slight-angle|slightly off]] the one the model uses would still look clean at high activations and muddled at low ones.

### A cheaper measure, and the control it loses

412 intervals is not a population, so the paper adds a scalable version [[automated-interpretability]]. Claude writes an explanation of a unit from examples where it fires. Then it predicts that unit's activations on unseen text from that explanation alone. What makes this a test is [[no-activation-leakage]]: no true activation reaches the prediction step except through the words. Scoring is the rank correlation between predicted and true activations [[activation-prediction-scoring]] — median 0.58 for features against 0.2 for neurons [[fig-40]]. A second run asks, from the explanation alone, which unseen tokens a unit promotes: 0.74 for features, 0.58 for neurons, chance 0.5 [[automated-logit-scoring]].

Both say features beat neurons, at different prices. Neither settles everything [[interpretability-evaluation-caveats]]: most real activations are small, landing in the bands that score worst [[low-interval-activation-skew]], and features were sampled without regard to importance [[interpretability-importance-caveat]].

Then the control the paper cares most about [[model-vs-data-question]]. Run [[dictionary-learning|dictionary learning]] on a transformer whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled [[randomized-transformer]], and those features score a slightly higher automated median than the real ones [[fig-70]]. The paper does not explain that away. It splits them [[randomized-feature-bimodality|into two clusters]] and shows the advantage comes from trivially scorable [[single-token-features]]; on everything else the real features win and the randomized ones sit where polysemantic neurons do. Its other answer: downstream effects were never an input to the autoencoder, and pinning a feature high makes the model generate matching text [[fig-43]].

### How much of the layer is accounted for

Finally, splice the reconstruction in for the real MLP activations [[loss-recovered-by-features]]. Loss rises; divide that rise by the rise from deleting the MLP outright [[zero-ablation-baseline]]; it comes to 21%, so 79% is called recovered. A wider dictionary or a weaker penalty pushes it to 94.5%, paid for in [[l0-norm|features active per token]].

The paper attaches its own warnings [[loss-recovery-caveats]]: fraction-of-loss may be the wrong framing, the features are not fully monosemantic, and the ablated-MLP denominator is probably [[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat|too generous]].

You can now ask of any feature how it would have scored, and read 79% as a ratio to a bad baseline rather than a verdict.

[[dictionary-learning]] turned up a feature that fires on Arabic script. That could be a fact about how one-layer transformers represent this data, or it could be an accident of one training run and one autoencoder. [[universality]] is the name for that question, and this theme is the paper's attempt to answer it.

Answering it needs something to compare against. So the paper trains [[transformer-a-and-b|a second transformer]] with the same architecture, the same Pile data and the same hyperparameters, differing only in the random seed. It then runs dictionary learning on that model's activations separately, giving a second dictionary, B/1.

Now [[feature-universality]] has a concrete shape. Does A/1/3450 have a counterpart in B/1, and can we say so without appealing to either dictionary's own indexing?

### Two ways to compare, and they disagree

The first answer treats a feature as a function on data. Represent it by the vector of its activations across 40,960,000 tokens, and call a feature's counterpart the one whose vector has the highest Pearson correlation. That is [[activation-similarity]], and for the Arabic feature it picks out B/1/1334 at 0.91 ([[fig-19]]).

Run that match for every feature in A/1 and the median is 0.72. On its own that number is hard to read. So the paper matches raw MLP neurons across the same two transformers the same way, and gets a median of 0.46 ([[feature-vs-neuron-universality]], [[fig-52]]). The comparison is what carries the claim: whatever dictionary learning recovers reproduces across seeds better than the neuron basis does.

The second answer treats a feature as a thing that does something. Correlate the two features' [[logit-weight|logit weight]] vectors, one entry per vocabulary token — that is [[logit-weight-similarity]]. For the Arabic pair it gives 0.23, against an activation correlation of 0.91 ([[fig-51]]), and the gap turns out to be widespread ([[fig-53]]).

The sharpest case is [[logit-weight-disagreement|A/1/3949 and B/1/3321]]: correlated 0.98 on activations, negatively correlated on logit weights, and both firing on PLOS journal abbreviations in citations while predicting the period that follows.

The paper does not read that as two different features. Its explanation is that the logit weight vector is a noisy way to compare: most of its entries sit in a large near-zero mode the paper hypothesizes is [[weight-interference|interference]] forced by [[superposition]], weights the model would probably prefer to be zero but cannot make zero. Correlating the whole vocabulary lets that mode set the score.

So the paper builds a third measure that weights each logit effect by whether it mattered. For each sampled datapoint, multiply the feature's activation there by its logit weight on the token that actually came next ([[eq-attribution-vector]]); stack those numbers into an [[attribution-vector]] and correlate. That is [[attribution-similarity]], and it is offered as a cheap stand-in for computing ablation effects everywhere, which would be the real measure.

It tracks activation similarity closely ([[fig-54]]). That agreement is the paper's stated justification for using activation correlation throughout the rest of the work.

### Beyond the twin model

Two models with identical architecture and identical data is the weakest form of the question. [[universality-with-the-literature|The stronger version]] asks whether these features resemble units other researchers reported in other models — base64 and all-caps units from earlier work, features found by [[sparse-probing]], region features that vaguely mirror [[multimodal-neurons]]. That comparison is done by eye rather than by correlation, and the paper says where the parallels fail.

You can now read the universality panel on any individual feature and know what its number means. The open question the paper hands forward is what the low-correlation pairs are: it guesses different [[feature-splitting|feature splittings]], or different [[true-features]] in the two models.

With thousands of features in hand, the question changes. The paper stops asking whether one feature is real and asks what the whole collection is like: which shapes recur, how features combine, and whether the list is a fixed answer at all.

### The kinds that keep coming back

A few shapes recur often enough that the paper names them as [[feature-motifs|motifs]]. [[context-features]] fire across a whole stretch of text of one kind — a DNA string, a base64 blob, Arabic script — rather than on one token type. [[token-in-context-features]] are narrower: one token, but only in one setting, like "the" in mathematics or "<" in HTML. One run has over a hundred features for "the" alone, more than the authors expected.

Two other shapes reach across positions. [[trigram-features]] implement a short fixed continuation, such as predicting "19" after "COVID-". [[memorization-features|Sequence-memorizing features]] go further, reproducing a long specific phrase, and show up only in large dictionaries.

All of them have a second reading. In a one-layer model the only MLP is the last one, so a feature's effect on the logits is close to linear, and the paper reads every feature as [[action-features|an action as well as a detector]]. A [[base64-feature]] detects base64. It also pushes base64 tokens up.

That reading is what makes the next motif possible. [[finite-state-automata-features|Automata-like assemblies]] are groups of features where one raises the probability of tokens that then switch on the next feature a position later. The simplest case is [[self-exciting-feature-loop|a feature that re-excites itself]] ([[fig-55]]). Four features chain into [[html-feature-automaton|a loop that emits well-formed HTML]] ([[fig-58]]). Nothing tied those four together during training. They interact through the sampled token stream, because HTML in the data has that shape.

### A zoom level, not a final list

Widen the autoencoder and the features do not claim new territory. They subdivide. The paper calls this [[feature-splitting]]. One feature for mathematical prose becomes separate features for category theory, complex analysis and field theory ([[fig-46]]). A "fires on the letter P" feature that looked like a bug becomes sixteen or more P-in-a-context features ([[fig-47]]).

That suggests a conjecture: some idealized set of [[true-features|features the model actually uses]] sits in tight superposition, and a narrow dictionary cannot separate them. It returns features covering roughly the same ground while being less specific. So dictionary width reads as [[dictionary-resolution|a resolution setting]] rather than a guess at a correct count. A small dictionary is a usable summary, not a wrong answer.

Splitting also raises a worry the paper leaves open. Giving "the in Physics" its own unit is [[local-vs-compositional-codes|a local code]]; representing "the" and "Physics" separately is a compositional one. [[are-token-in-context-features-real|Which one the transformer itself uses]] is unsettled, since the L1 penalty may be buying sparsity by imposing [[local-code|one unit per token-context pair]]. The reason to think the local code is at least partly real is [[sharper-predictions-argument|that a compositional code forces the logits to be a sum of two generic contributions]], and the model may want something sharper.

### What the geometry forces

Feature directions carry this too. Related features sit at small angles, so [[feature-geometry-clusters|families are tight geometric clumps]] in [[feature-umap|a 2-D projection of the directions]] ([[fig-44]]).

The picture the authors brought from Toy Models had features spread roughly evenly, pushed apart by interference. Clumping does not fit it. So they revise: [[theories-of-superposition|superposition is denser and more structured than the toy picture]], perhaps because related features fire together, more likely because they share downstream actions. Features may also not be one-dimensional intensity scales at all — [[feature-manifolds|continuous higher-dimensional patches]] ([[fig-61]]) would make "the [[correct-number-of-features]]" not a well-posed question. The paper offers this as speculation, not result.

You can now take any single feature and ask which motif it belongs to, what it hands off to, and at what resolution you are seeing it. What none of that tells you is whether the dictionary itself is any good.
