pages.body:
Which of the trained autoencoders do you keep? The property the paper wants — a dictionary whose features a person can read — has no cheap measurement, so [[evaluating-dictionary-learning|the evaluation]] is a bundle of imperfect substitutes for one slow judgment.

That slow judgment is [[manual-inspection]]: open a feature, look at the text it fires on, and ask whether one description covers all of it. It is subjective, and it does not scale. Everything else here is a proxy standing in for it, and the paper says plainly that it never found a satisfactory single metric. On synthetic data the problem goes away, since [[toy-model-ground-truth|toy models]] are built with known features and recovery can be checked directly, but the transformer is not a toy model.

The first attempt was to skip proxies entirely. [[information-based-metric|An information-based score]] would pick the factorization minimizing the total information of the autoencoder plus the data. It failed in a way worth keeping: a run where hundreds of features fired on every token, but reconstruction error was low, could score better than a much sparser run. The metric rewarded the density the paper was trying to avoid.

### Sparsity against explained behavior

That failure is why sparsity is measured directly rather than inferred. The [[l0-norm|$L^0$ norm]] is the average number of features nonzero on a token. The paper has no principled target and says so. It aims for under 10 or 20, and distrusts runs where $L^0$ is a large fraction of the 512-dimensional activation being decomposed.

Sparsity on its own is trivial to win, since a dictionary that outputs nothing is perfectly sparse. So it is read against [[loss-recovered-by-features|how much of the MLP layer's loss contribution survives substitution]]: splice the reconstruction back into the transformer and see what the loss does. [[l0-nll-tradeoff|Plotting one against the other]] across runs turns hyperparameter choice into a picture, [[fig-68]]. The four [[l1-coefficient|L1 coefficients]] land as four vertical bands, so the penalty largely fixes the sparsity level, while widening the dictionary climbs a band at nearly constant sparsity.

This is also why [[training-loss-metric|training loss]] cannot arbitrate. Changing the L1 coefficient changes the loss function, so the numbers are not comparable across the runs you most want to compare.

### What the density histogram shows

[[feature-density]] is the fraction of tokens on which a feature is nonzero, and it is the quick proxy the paper reaches for most. Plot every feature of a run by density on a log axis and the distribution usually splits into two humps, [[fig-64]].

Almost every feature in the right hump, the [[high-density-cluster]], reads as interpretable. Almost none in the left one, the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], do; these fire on fewer than roughly one token in a million. The paper treats that left hump as an artifact of autoencoder training rather than anything the transformer computes, and says it is still investigating where it comes from.

At the largest dictionary sizes with a high L1 coefficient the two humps merge, [[fig-65]]. [[density-cluster-separation|Adding two more per-feature numbers]] — the encoder bias, and the dot product of a feature's encoder and decoder vectors — pulls the high-density cluster back out as a separate blob, [[fig-66]]. From these histograms the paper reads [[feature-density-diagnostics|three specific numbers]] and judges a run by them.

Densities this low have consequences elsewhere. Because features fire on $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$ of tokens, [[importance-scoring-degeneracy|reweighting interpretability scores toward random text]] mostly ends up rewarding the prediction of zero, [[fig-71]].

Manual inspection also needs somewhere to happen. The [[feature-exploration-interface]] publishes every feature of every run — where it fires, what it does to the logits, what ablating it costs, [[fig-4]].

You should now be able to read a density histogram and a sparsity frontier, and to ask what a given L1 coefficient bought. What you cannot do is what the paper cannot: [[recognizing-good-features|tell a good run from a bad one without looking at it]].

What exactly is a figure in this paper showing you, and what would that same picture look like if the claim under it were false? [[reading-the-evidence]] gathers the small set of shapes the paper reuses, in the order you meet them.

### Before there is a measurement

Two shapes arrive before any data does.

A [[conceptual-schematic]] is a drawing of a hypothesis, made where the paper has a claim but nothing measured yet. Its job is to fix what the claim would mean, as [[fig-3]] does for [[superposition]]. Nothing in it is evidence, so hold it against the measured figures that follow.

The [[feature-browser-screenshot]] is a screengrab of the published tool with arrows and captions added on top. One page there puts four kinds of evidence about a single feature side by side, so there is no one axis to read. Everything outside the grey panel is annotation the tool never prints.

### One feature at a time

The per-feature case is five claims ([[feature-evidence-template]]), and each claim has its own shape.

Specificity comes first, carried by the [[activation-spectrum-by-proxy]]. This is a histogram of one unit's activation values, with every column split by a [[computational-proxy]] computed independently of the feature. You read it by the proportion of colour within a column, not by how tall the column is. If the unit were [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]], that proportion would stay flat as you moved right rather than climbing toward the strongest firings.

That leaves the weak activations, which are most of the tokens. The [[activation-mass-expected-value-plot]] answers them by weighting each bin by activation magnitude, so a bar's height is total activation contributed rather than number of firings. In a one-layer model a feature's effect on the logits is close to linear in its activation, which is why that weighting tracks influence.

Downstream effect is shown twice over. The [[logit-weight-histogram]] gives one number per vocabulary entry, and the claim lives in the small second mode out in the right tail, not in the towering mode at zero. The [[annotated-dataset-example-panel]] then shows the causal version on real text, with orange shading for firing strength and a coloured underline for how far ablating the feature moved that token's predicted log-likelihood. That panel is read by inspection and count rather than by a statistic, and the paper says so.

The fourth claim, that [[feature-neuron-nonalignment|the feature is not a neuron]] in disguise, is the [[feature-direction-stem-plot]]: the decoder column drawn one MLP neuron at a time. One tall stem would mean a renamed neuron; spread across many is what superposition predicts.

### Whole dictionaries at once

The fifth claim, universality, turns from single features to populations, in the [[cross-model-agreement-population-scatter]]. Note which axis chose the pairs and which is then free to agree or not, because only the free axis is evidence.

The [[features-versus-neurons-score-histogram]] puts features and MLP neurons on one score and reads the overlap. [[interpretability-across-activation-bands]] asks whether that score survives outside the top-activating examples. The [[scoring-robustness-panel-grid]] crosses several invented scores against several populations, including a [[randomized-transformer]] control that beats the real features on one of them.

Geometry follows. The [[umap-feature-map]] asks whether families found by reading text are also clumps of small angles, which is how [[feature-splitting]] becomes visible. The [[feature-relationship-graph]] carries claims that live between features rather than inside one.

Last come the training diagnostics, which judge a run before anyone has read a feature. The [[feature-density-histogram]] is read for its shape and its left edge: [[fig-64]] splits into a bulk mode and an [[ultralow-density-cluster]] the paper discards. When those modes overlap, the [[dictionary-geometry-diagnostic-scatter]] separates them on other per-feature numbers. The [[sparsity-versus-explained-loss-sweep]] prices the hyperparameters, one dot per trained autoencoder, [[l0-norm]] against recovered loss.

You can now ask of any figure here: which population is plotted, which axis selected the points and which was free, and what shape would appear if the claim failed.

pages.body:
The paper's case for dictionary learning is a case by elimination. Of the two routes out of superposition it inherited from its own earlier toy-model work, it argues the first is closed for a reason internal to the language modelling loss, so the second is what is left.

Start with the picture that creates the problem. [[superposition|Superposition]] is the hypothesis that a network represents more independent features than it has neurons, by giving each [[feature|feature]] its own direction in activation space rather than its own neuron. The proposed mechanism is [[noisy-simulation]]: the 512-neuron MLP under study approximately simulates a much larger and much sparser network [[fig-3]]. That works only because of [[feature-sparsity]] — few features are on at any one token.

Two consequences follow, and the paper needs both. The decomposition has to be [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]], meaning more feature directions than the 512 dimensions they live in. And more than 512 directions cannot all be mutually perpendicular, so some pairs have a nonzero dot product. Firing one feature then slightly fires its neighbours, which the paper calls [[interference]]. Sparsity is what keeps that cross-talk occasional rather than constant.

Superposition also accounts for the symptom. The neuron basis is a [[privileged-basis|privileged basis]] — singled out by the elementwise ReLU — so it was reasonable to hope neurons would be the features. [[polysemanticity|Polysemantic neurons]], which fire on unrelated things, say they are not.

### The route the paper closes

The first route was [[architectural-approaches-to-superposition|building models that lack superposition]]. The authors tried [[activation-sparsity-training|training the subject model for activation sparsity]], as far as one-hot activations. That does remove superposition. It does not deliver [[monosemanticity]].

The reason is [[cross-entropy-favors-polysemanticity|a four-feature calculation]]. Take one binary neuron and four mutually exclusive features A, B, C, D, each predicting its own token. If the neuron fires on A alone and predicts A, then on the three-quarters of tokens where it is silent the model can only guess uniformly among B, C, D, costing $\ln 3$ each time: $\tfrac{3}{4}\ln 3 \approx 0.8$. If instead it fires ambiguously on A and B, predicting uniform over {A, B}, and predicts uniform over {C, D} when silent, every token costs $\ln 2 \approx 0.7$.

The ambiguous neuron wins. Under [[mse-loss-and-monosemanticity|mean squared error]] prior work finds the two solutions can tie, or the clean one can win — but language models are trained with cross-entropy. [[solu|SoLU]], an earlier attempt to pull features onto the neuron basis, is reported to help some neurons and hurt others.

### Why the solver is deliberately weak

That leaves [[dictionary-learning]]: write each activation as a sparse combination drawn from a larger-than-necessary set of directions. Asking for sparsity is licensed by borrowing [[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables|a long-standing hypothesis]] about natural data, not derived from the transformer. Overcompleteness is what separates this from [[disentanglement]], which seeks at most as many factors as dimensions, and it turns the inner problem into [[compressed-sensing]], [[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery|NP-hard]] in exact form.

Hence the argument for weakness: a solver strong enough to succeed at an NP-hard recovery is doing something the transformer certainly is not, so [[weak-dictionary-learning|it might dig out structure the model cannot read]]. [[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms|Established iterative methods]] are set aside, and a [[sparse-autoencoder]] with an [[l1-sparsity-penalty|L1 penalty]] is used instead — architecturally close to an MLP layer, and able to run over 8 billion activation vectors [[table-1]]. Its reconstruction term is MSE, which the paper notes should stop the dictionary itself going [[superposition-all-the-way-down|into superposition]].

### How much of this is shown

The four-feature calculation is exact but tiny: one binary neuron, four features, hand-chosen predictions. The step from it to "cross-entropy models generally prefer polysemanticity" is stated as a belief, supported by experiments whose results are not reported here in numbers. The SoLU trade-off is asserted without a total accounting.

The weakness argument is an argument by analogy. Architectural similarity between a one-hidden-layer ReLU autoencoder and an MLP layer is not a demonstration that their recovery powers match, and no head-to-head comparison against the classical methods is shown. Superposition itself remains a hypothesis throughout. This page is the paper's reasoning about what to try, not evidence that it worked.

The method is one loss function with two terms, and one scalar setting the rate of exchange between them. The paper has no single number telling it where to set that scalar, or whether a finished run came out well, so it triangulates from several proxies it calls imperfect.

Start with the shape of the answer. [[linear-feature-decomposition|The decomposition]] writes each MLP activation vector as a fixed bias plus a weighted sum of unit vectors, one term per feature ([[eq-feature-decomposition]]). Written that way, a feature is a direction by construction. That is [[linear-representation-hypothesis|an assumption carried in before any fitting happens]] — if the model held some property in another form, this factorization has nowhere to put it.

The [[sparse-autoencoder]] is the paper's way of obtaining one. Its wide ReLU hidden layer supplies the weights; [[eq-encoder]] fixes what a [[feature-activation|feature activation]] is, one non-negative number per dictionary element. The columns of the [[dictionary-decoder|output matrix]] supply the [[feature-direction|directions]].

Training is [[eq-autoencoder-loss|two terms and no more]]: the [[mse-reconstruction-term|squared error]] between an activation and its reconstruction, plus an [[l1-sparsity-penalty|L1 penalty]] on the hidden activations scaled by [[l1-coefficient|$\lambda$]]. The first term is cheapest when many features are on. The second charges for every unit of activation, which drives most feature activations to exactly zero, and that is what buys sparsity.

The penalty has an obvious loophole. Halve every activation, double the matching decoder column, and the reconstruction is unchanged while the penalty falls. [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns|Holding every column to $L^2$ norm 1]] closes it.

### Setting the coefficient without a metric

So where does $\lambda$ go? [[training-loss-metric|Training loss]] is the cheapest signal and it is useless here, because changing $\lambda$ changes the function being measured. An [[information-based-metric|information-theoretic score]] the authors tried rewarded dense solutions, and was dropped.

Plot every trained autoencoder by its [[l0-norm|average number of features active per token]] against the [[loss-recovered-by-features|fraction of the MLP layer's loss contribution it recovers]], and the runs lie on a [[l0-nll-tradeoff|frontier]] ([[fig-68]]). The coefficient is then chosen by eye off that frontier. The paper says it knows no principled sparsity target, and reports only a rough preference for fewer than ten or twenty active features per token.

The recovered fraction is itself a ratio. Splicing the reconstruction in for the real activations raises the model's loss by some amount; divide that by the loss increase from deleting the MLP outright ([[zero-ablation-baseline]]). For run A/1 the numerator is 21% of the denominator, so 79% is called recovered. A/5, with 131,072 features and a lower coefficient, reaches 94.5% while firing far more features per token.

### What the numbers do not show

The paper flags its own weak points. It says the ablated-MLP denominator may be an especially bad baseline, so 79% is likely inflated. It also measures reconstruction, not interpretation: [[explanation-based-loss-measure|simulating activations from each feature's written explanation]] would measure the thing wanted, at an estimated $12,500–$25,000 for 100k features over one 4096-token context, so it is not run.

The other main proxy is qualitative. A log-scale [[feature-density|density histogram]] of run A/16 splits into two humps ([[fig-64]]). Almost every feature in the [[high-density-cluster|right mode]] is reported interpretable and almost none in the [[ultralow-density-cluster|left]], which the paper reads as a training artifact and says it is still investigating. In A/1 that reading discards 292 features as [[de-facto-dead-neurons|effectively dead]], on top of 168 that a zero-activity check already caught. That split is stated anecdotally, with no scoring behind it — weaker than the use it is put to. When the modes overlap, [[density-cluster-separation|two further per-feature numbers separate them]], one of which carries information only because the [[untied-decoder-weights|encoder was learned independently of the decoder]].

My reading, not the paper's: nothing here measures the step from "$L^0$ under twenty" to "features a person can interpret". The one outside check, [[external-replication|an invited researcher]] finding 92% of his learned directions spread across many neurons ([[fig-63]]), speaks to features not being neurons, not to whether a run was well chosen.

The paper's case that a feature responds to one thing rests on a score computed without ever looking at the feature. That score carries the argument, and it is also the soft spot: wherever the score and the feature disagree, the paper mostly decides the score is the one that is wrong.

[[activation-specificity]] asks whether a feature being on implies the hypothesized context is present. The paper ranks it above [[activation-sensitivity]], which asks the converse — whether the feature is on whenever the context is there. The reason is that [[polysemanticity]] shows up as one unit firing on clearly unrelated things, so a feature that misses some Arabic text is merely incomplete, while a feature that fires on Arabic and on Python is the failure the method exists to rule out.

Specificity is the first claim in [[feature-evidence-template|the template each case study is walked through]], and establishing it needs a way to label text as Arabic that does not come from the feature.

### Building the yardstick

That labelling is the [[computational-proxy]]. Every proxy has the same shape, [[eq-proxy-loglikelihood-ratio|fixed by one equation]]: [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy|the log of how much likelier a string is under a guessed context than under text in general]]. The denominator is [[unigram-p-s-estimate|a product of per-token unigram probabilities]]. The numerator is the hard term, obtained two ways.

For a writing system, $P(s \mid \text{Arabic})$ would otherwise mean building a generative model of Arabic text. [[script-proxy-via-bayes|Bayes' rule]] [[eq-bayes-script-proxy|inverts it]] into $P(\text{Arabic} \mid s)$, which is a lookup rather than a model: [[unicode-block-detection|does each codepoint sit in an Arabic block]] such as U+0600–U+06FF. [[arabic-script-proxy|The Arabic proxy]] is that inversion carried out.

For character sets there is no script to look up, so [[character-distribution-proxy|the string is modelled as a uniform draw over the allowed alphabet]] — $1/64$ per character for [[base64-proxy|base64]], $1/4$ for [[dna-proxy|DNA]].

### What it shows, and what it does not

Splitting a feature's activation histogram by the proxy gives a spectrum rather than a verdict. In [[fig-8]], Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens but 81% of tokens where [[arabic-script-feature|A/1/3450]] is active — 98% of those above activation 5, and only 25% where the feature barely fires.

The low end is impure, and the paper does not clean it up. It argues instead that [[large-activations-dominate|the low end matters less]], because in this one-layer model [[linear-logit-effects|a feature's effect on the logits is linear in its activation]], up to layer norm rescaling. Twice the activation is twice the push. The [[expected-value-plot]] re-weights each bar by activation magnitude on that reasoning, and [[fig-9]] then puts almost all the mass on Arabic. That is a claim about weighting, not about purity — and the paper says the same linearity claim in deeper models rests on conjecture.

Folded into one number, the [[feature-proxy-correlation]] is a [[pearson-correlation|linear correlation]] between feature and proxy: 0.74 for Arabic over 40 million tokens, 0.8 for the binarized [[dna-feature|DNA proxy]] ([[fig-20]]), 0.55 for [[hebrew-feature|Hebrew]] against [[hebrew-script-proxy|its Unicode score]] ([[fig-33]]), and 0.38 for [[base64-feature|base64]] ([[fig-25]]).

### Where the argument thins out

The last two are where the yardstick contradicts the feature, and the paper answers by arguing against the yardstick. It keeps [[proxy-limitations|a catalog of proxy failures]]: hexadecimal strings satisfy a random draw from [a-zA-Z0-9+/] but are handled by [[hexadecimal-feature|a feature of their own]]; a space inside the triplets TGG AGT breaks the strict ATCG vocabulary; the feature fires on the `'-` in 5'-TCT because DNA follows.

The readings are defensible one by one. But the audit behind them, [[fig-21]], is a small grid of hand-read examples, adjudicated by the authors about their own features. Nothing independent settles whether 0.38 means a broad proxy or an impure feature — that reading is mine, not a hedge the paper states — and the paper's reason for choosing the first is that it happened to find a hexadecimal feature.

The sensitivity half is left frankly incomplete. A/1/3450 skips the definite-article prefix "ال" entirely, and the gap is filled by [[complementary-arabic-features|other Arabic features]] rather than closed.

The autoencoder is fit to MLP activation vectors and to nothing else. So what a feature does further along in the network — which logits it raises, which predictions break without it — was never an input to the fit, and the paper turns that omission into evidence.

The worry it answers is [[model-vs-data-question|whether features tell us about the model or the data]]. Activations carry both the dataset's regularities and the model's transformation of them, so an interpretable-looking feature could be a dataset correlation projected into a new basis. But [[activations-only-decomposition|fitting activations only]] means the second half of the model — the MLP down-projection and the unembedding — is held out. If a feature's downstream behaviour still matches the interpretation read off when it fires, that match has to be a property of the model. That is [[downstream-effects-outside-dictionary-learning|the argument]].

### Three probes, each stronger than the last

The cheapest probe is the [[logit-weight]]: one number per vocabulary token, saying how much the feature's firing moves that token's next-token logit. A single vector can stand for the effect only if the effect scales with the activation instead of changing shape as it grows, which the paper argues holds in a one-layer model ([[linear-logit-effects]]). The path from a [[feature-direction]] to the logits also runs through the final layer norm, which is not linear, so the paper replaces it with a fixed mean-removing projection plus a diagonal scaling ([[layer-norm-linearization]]). What remains is a product of matrices, $\mathbf{d}_i W_{down}\pi L W_{unembed}$, median-centred because softmax has no absolute logit scale.

For the [[arabic-script-feature]] the resulting histogram has two humps ([[fig-10]]): a fat one at zero and a small one far right, holding Arabic characters and the byte tokens \xd8 and \xd9 that open most Arabic UTF-8 encodings. This shape recurs across features ([[logit-weight-second-mode]]). The paper lists three ways this linear approximation could overstate real influence, so the histogram alone is a suggestion, not a causal claim.

The second probe measures rather than approximates. [[feature-ablation]] subtracts the feature's own contribution — its activation times its dictionary direction — from the activations and finishes the forward pass ([[eq-feature-ablation]]). Note what is not subtracted: this is [[directional-ablation|removal along one direction]], leaving every other feature's contribution in place — which names something specific only because the decomposition is [[linear-feature-decomposition|a bias plus a weighted sum of unit directions]]. Ablation lowers the model's probability on Arabic-script tokens across the feature's whole activation range, and the only tokens it helps are punctuation shared with other scripts ([[fig-11]]).

The third probe is [[pinned-feature-sampling]]: hold the feature at its maximum observed value, touch nothing else, and sample. From the prefix 1,2,3,...,10 the continuation comes out in Arabic ([[fig-12]]). This is the steering affordance the paper claims a good decomposition should give you ([[uses-of-a-feature-decomposition]]), repeated for other features ([[fig-43]]).

### Where the evidence thins

Pinning is one hand-chosen prompt on one hand-chosen feature. It shows the effect exists; it measures nothing about how often it holds.

A separate leg checks that [[dictionary-learning]] did not just rename a neuron ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]). The feature's direction spreads over 27 of 512 neurons with coefficients above 0.1, and its three largest coefficients are negative ([[fig-13]]). That rules out one neuron, not a small cancelling set — which is why the paper also inspects the [[most-correlated-neuron]], A/neurons/489, and finds it firing on a mixture of non-English languages with Arabic a thin sliver ([[fig-14]]). The account offered, that near-mutually-exclusive features are [[mutually-exclusive-features-in-superposition|cheap to superpose]], is an interpretation of that picture rather than something the figure tests.

One hypothesis is carrying weight quietly. The tall central mode of near-zero logit weights is read as [[weight-interference|crosstalk forced by superposition]] rather than anything the model wants. That reading is what lets the paper discount low cross-model agreement on logit weights while the matched Arabic pair's activations correlate at 0.91 — and it is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

pages.body:
The argument is that a feature recovered by [[dictionary-learning|dictionary learning]] is a fact about what a one-layer transformer learned, not an artifact of one training run or one autoencoder fit. The test is repetition: train a second transformer that differs only in random seed, give it its own dictionary, and ask whether the same features come back.

The worry this answers is real. The [[sparse-autoencoder|sparse autoencoder]] sees only MLP activations, and its objective is reconstruction error plus a penalty on the sum of hidden activations. A wide enough dictionary trained that way will always return some set of directions that reconstructs the activations sparsely. Nothing in the loss requires those directions to be the ones the model itself uses. Agreement across seeds is a check the method cannot perform on itself.

So the paper needs [[transformer-a-and-b|a second transformer]]. Model B is another instance of the same [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|testbed]] — same 128-dimensional residual stream, same 512-neuron MLP, same Pile data, same hyperparameters — reseeded. Its dictionaries are trained separately, on activations from different tokens.

Matching then needs a way to name a feature without reference to either model's weights. The paper's answer is [[activation-similarity]]: write a feature as the vector of its activations over a fixed set of 40,960,000 tokens, and call two features counterparts when that vector has the highest [[pearson-correlation]] between them. This is a best-match search, run once per feature.

The [[arabic-script-feature|Arabic feature]] A/1/3450 finds B/1/1334 at a correlation of 0.91 [[fig-19]]. Then the population version: every feature in A/1 matched into B/1, and every neuron in A matched into B the same way. The median feature match is 0.72; the median neuron match is 0.46 [[fig-52]]. That gap is the paper's strongest quantitative claim that [[feature-vs-neuron-universality|features are more universal than neurons]].

### Where the agreement breaks

Firing alike is not acting alike. A feature's [[logit-weight|logit weight]] vector says how much its firing moves each vocabulary token's next-token logit, and correlating those vectors gives [[logit-weight-similarity]]. For the Arabic pair it is 0.23, against 0.91 on activations. The sharpest case in [[fig-53]] is A/1/3949 and B/1/3321: correlated 0.98 on activations, negatively on logit weights, though both fire on PLoS journal abbreviations in citations and predict the period that follows.

The paper's explanation is [[weight-interference]]. Under [[superposition]] a model packs more features into the layer than it has neurons, so feature directions cannot be orthogonal and each feature writes small unwanted amounts to tokens it does not care about. Those near-zero entries are the large central cloud, and they dominate the correlation.

[[attribution-similarity]] is the paper's way around this. For each sampled token it builds an [[attribution-vector|attribution score]] — the feature's activation there, times its logit weight on the token that actually came next [[eq-attribution-vector]] — so entries where the feature was silent, or where the token never occurred, stop counting. Correlations of those vectors track activation similarity closely [[fig-54]], which is the paper's justification for using activation correlation throughout.

### What this does not settle

Model B differs from model A only in seed. The paper says plainly that this is the most minimal form of universality available. The stronger form — [[universality-with-the-literature|matching against units other researchers found]], such as the [[solu-base64-neuron|base64 neuron reported in a SoLU model]] — is qualitative resemblance between visualizations, with no correlation computed.

Three further gaps. Weight interference is offered as a hypothesis and not tested here. The attribution measure is built out of the same logit weights whose disagreement it repairs, so it is not an independent second measurement. And the low-correlation tail is attributed to [[feature-splitting]] or to genuinely different learned features, which the paper does not distinguish.

One reading of my own: A/1 holds thousands of features against 512 neurons, so the feature search has far more candidates to find a best match among. Some of the 0.72-against-0.46 gap may be that asymmetry rather than universality.

The four features studied in depth were chosen because a cheap independent check existed for them, so the paper needs different evidence before it can say anything about features in general. That second body of evidence — one human rubric and two automated scores — puts features ahead of neurons every time, but each measure is thinner than the case studies, and two of the paper's own controls push back.

[[cherry-picked-case-studies|The case studies were cherry-picked]], and the paper says so outright. Arabic script, DNA, base64 and Hebrew each admit a [[computational-proxy]] — a cheap per-token score for how likely a string is to come from that context. No such score can be built for "text concerning fantasy games". [[global-analysis-framing|Section 4 swaps the evidence]]: features sampled uniformly from the run, judged by a person and by a language model. The deep evidence and the representative evidence are never available for the same feature.

### The three measures

Reading a unit's [[top-dataset-examples]] flatters it, because even a mixed neuron looks coherent at its maximum — the paper calls this a weakness in its own earlier work. Each unit's range from zero to its maximum is instead cut into eleven evenly spaced bands, and examples are drawn from every band. One band is an [[activation-interval]], and intervals, not units, get scored.

[[manual-interpretability-scoring|The human scoring]] covers 412 such intervals across 162 features and neurons, on a 0–14 rubric covering confidence in an interpretation, consistency of the activations and logit weights, and specificity. The two distributions barely overlap [[fig-39]]. Median neuron: 0, meaning no hypothesis could be formed at all. Median feature interval: 12. The paper trusts this measure most. It is one annotator, an author, blinded only to which kind of unit he was seeing.

[[automated-interpretability]] buys scale instead. Claude writes an explanation of a unit from examples where it fires, and a separate pass then predicts that unit's activations from the explanation alone. [[no-activation-leakage|Nothing else about the activations reaches the prediction step]], so the score measures how much of the unit survived that written description. [[activation-prediction-scoring|The score]] is a [[spearman-correlation]] over 60 nine-token examples — 540 predictions per feature [[fig-40]]. [[automated-logit-scoring|A companion test]] asks which unseen tokens the unit promotes, scored against a 50/50 mix of top positive logit tokens and random ones: chance is 50%, features average 74%, neurons 58% [[fig-41]]. Neurons land above chance, so that is a margin, not a clean separation.

### Where the argument bends

Two controls cut the other way, and the paper reports both.

Run [[dictionary-learning]] on [[randomized-transformer|the same model with the entries of each weight matrix shuffled]] — [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|same shapes and data]], no learned computation left — and its features take a slightly higher median automated activation score than the real ones [[fig-70]]. The paper's response is to split the randomized features into a single-token cluster and a polysemantic one, after which the real features win on the second. That split is post hoc, and the headline disagreement stands as stated.

[[importance-scoring]] is the principled fix for the fact that the scored examples were not sampled at random: random tokens get weight 1, interval tokens a weight proportional to how often the feature fires. Applying it collapses most feature scores toward zero, leaving a median of 0.28 against 0.04 for neurons [[fig-71]]. [[importance-scoring-degeneracy|The reason is density, not quality]]: with [[feature-density|densities]] running from about $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$, nearly all the weight lands on random text, where 88% of a feature's true activations are zero against 54% for neurons. Predicting zero everywhere then scores well.

A third strain is internal. Scoring each band separately turns interpretability into a curve [[activation-interval-analysis]], and strong activations hold up far better than weak ones [[fig-42]]. But [[low-interval-activation-skew|most real activations are small]] and land in exactly the bands that score worst. The paper's answer is that [[large-activations-dominate|strong activations carry most of a feature's effect on the logits]] — an argument, not a measurement of what is left unexplained.

The paper turns from single features to the whole population, and makes a claim in two halves. Dictionary width is a resolution setting rather than a count of the model's parts; and at any resolution, the features that come back have kinds and a geometry the authors' earlier theory of superposition did not predict.

[[feature-splitting]] is the first half. Add hidden units to the autoencoder and the new dictionary directions do not go off to cover parts of activation space that nothing covered before. They subdivide ground already covered.

Take base64. In A/0, the 512-feature dictionary, one feature fires across every token of a base64 string. In A/1, with 4,096 features, three cover those same tokens: one prefers letters ([[base64-feature|A/1/2357]]), one prefers digits ([[base64-digit-feature|A/1/2364]]), one fires on base64 that decodes to readable ASCII ([[fig-48]]). What looked like [[multiple-features-for-one-context]] — a redundancy bug — is splitting seen from below.

[[fig-46]] repeats this for technical writing across three widths, linking features by [[masked-cosine-similarity|masked cosine similarity]]: cosine similarity of two features' activations over tokens where at least one of them fires. The refinement is a graph, not a tree: features both split and merge across widths. The 0.4 connection threshold was picked for readability, so it illustrates splitting rather than measuring it.

From this the paper reaches [[dictionary-resolution]]. It conjectures a set of [[true-features]] the model actually uses, packed too tightly in superposition for a narrow dictionary to separate. If that holds, the [[correct-number-of-features]] matters less than it first appears. And features the dictionary missed would smear across the ones it learned as weak, impure activations — [[autoencoder-width-limitation]].

### The kinds that recur

Two motifs dominate. [[context-features]] fire across a whole stretch of text of a certain kind, such as the [[dna-feature|DNA feature]] on runs of A, T, C and G. [[token-in-context-features]] fire on one token in one setting; A/4 holds over a hundred features for the word "the" alone.

Every feature also reads as an action, since a one-layer MLP writes almost linearly to the output ([[action-features]]). Read that way through the [[logit-weight]] — one number per vocabulary token — chains appear. [[finite-state-automata-features]] are assemblies where one feature raises the probability of tokens that make the next fire a position later; [[fig-58]] traces four A/0 features generating valid HTML. They meet through the token stream rather than having been learned together, and the handoffs are read off visualisations and logit weights rather than tested by ablation — so the automaton is a description rather than a demonstration.

Some of it belongs to the tokenizer. [[byte-pair-encoding]] merges frequent byte sequences, so one non-Latin character often arrives as several tokens ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]) — the prefix-suffix pairs that [[unicode-token-state-machines]] are built from. The digit feature pushes digit tokens down, because two adjacent digits would have merged into one ([[fig-49]], [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]]). My reading: that much is a fact about the encoding, not the model.

### What the paper cannot settle

Hundreds of token-in-context features amount to a [[local-code]] — one unit per combination of properties — where a [[compositional-code]] would keep "the" and "physics" as separate units. The paper suspects its own method: a local code is sparser, and the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] rewards sparsity. Against that it sets the [[sharper-predictions-argument]]: a compositional code forces the logits after "the" in physics to be the sum of two generic contributions, and a model wanting sharper predictions has no other route. That is an argument about what is achievable, not a measurement; the paper claims only that it holds "to some extent".

The geometry is the other loose end. Related features sit at small angles, so families found by reading text are tight clusters in a projection of dictionary directions ([[fig-44]], [[feature-geometry-clusters]]) — though UMAP preserves local neighbourhoods and not global distances, so it supports the clustering claim only. Clumping is not what the [[isotropic-superposition-model]] predicts, so [[theories-of-superposition]] is revised. Whether the cause is [[correlated-features]] or [[action-sharing-features]] is open; the paper leans to the second. And if [[feature-manifolds]] exist, the number of features may not be a well-posed question.
